lines: A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.
+- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info`, `/pair` and the web page's three files, which are constant and carry nothing of the host.

- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.

- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.

- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.

- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. A native client sends it only as a bearer header over the pinned connection; it is never in a URL.
- **A browser (2026-10-23).** The QR's URL opens the port's page. The code is in the fragment, which no request carries, so it reaches no server before the page has read `/info` and compared its `spki_sha256` and `server_id` with the fragment's; the page then clears the fragment (`history.replaceState`) and pairs with `transport: "cookie"`. The reply sets `__Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` and leaves the token out of its body, so the page's script never holds it; the host reads the bearer if there is one, else the cookie of exactly its own name. Cookies ignore ports, which is why the name carries the server id: two instances on one address keep one cookie each. A request authenticated by the cookie alone that is not a `GET`, or is an upgrade, must carry `Origin: https://<its Host header>` or is refused 403 `origin`; a bearer request needs none. The page keeps only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}` in `localStorage`, which is public and lets it tell a later 401 apart through `/info`: the same key and id say the device was removed on the host, a different one says the identity changed. The comparison is not a defence in a browser: a page cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key. It catches a QR for another host or a stale one. The trust step is the owner proceeding past the browser's certificate warning, which the dialog says to do only if the address is this Mac's and only on a network they trust; the code is single-use, so a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing. lines: - **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying the page's URL, `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>` (an older host carried `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}` as JSON, and the Swift client parses both), and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. Before pairing, `/info` is served to any client and nothing in it is trusted; after pairing, every connection verifies the pin before the token is presented.

- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.

- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
-- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Serve a web control surface from the remote port, paired from a URL whose fragment carries the code

The port answers GET /, /app.js and /app.css (web/, built in by
adapters/web.rs) to anyone, on the connection thread, with a strict
content security policy and Connection: close, under a window of 120
a minute. The invite the QR and "Copy invite" carry is the page's URL
with the code, key and server id in the fragment, so no request
carries the code; a Mac-only port names the loopback and the dialog
says so. The page compares /info with the fragment, pairs with
transport "cookie", and gets its token as an HttpOnly, Secure,
SameSite=Strict cookie named __Host-sb-<server_id>, absent from the
body. A cookie-only write or upgrade must carry the page's Origin.
The page lists sessions waiting first, reads a session's last
response or screen, replies under control with an op kept across a
retry, and polls /waiting, the events socket only hastening it. The
Swift client parses the URL as well as the JSON invite. Spike 23
records five parallel connections against the four-slot pool; the
browser questions were not run.

Contract additions:
- No new AppAction or Effect variant, no port method.
- RemoteReply.headers, RemoteReply::new; RemoteRequest.{cookie,
  origin, host}.
- core::remote::invite_url.
- Wire: GET /api/v1/me; /pair request field transport; the
  __Host-sb-<server_id> cookie accepted as a credential beside the
  bearer header; the 403 code origin; GET /, /app.js, /app.css before
  pairing; the invite text is a URL (the JSON still parses in the
  Swift client).
- No change to model.rs, control/, or any schema version.
EOF
git status --short; git log --oneline -1

# Implement notes: sb-230, v5rev-opus-leanb

Branch `stage/sb-230-implement-v5rev-opus-leanb`, one commit as the plan
says:

- `4b3a20c` Serve a web control surface from the remote port, paired from
  a URL whose fragment carries the code (the plan's message, with the
  plan's contract list in the body). Not pushed, no PR.

Before the commit: `cargo fmt --all`, `cargo clippy --locked --workspace
--all-targets -- -D warnings` (clean), `cargo test --locked --workspace`
(all pass; `tests/remote.rs` 52, lib 536, ui 205). The pre-commit hook ran
too. `swift test --filter FixturesTests` passes (5 tests, the new URL
parse among them); the rest of the Swift suite was not run. No
`cfg(target_os)` arm was touched, so the Linux cross-clippy of `dispatch`
was not needed. `git status` is empty after the commit.

## What was built

- **Transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`).** `RemoteRequest` gains
  `cookie`, `origin`, `host` (read in `read_request`) and a
  `cookie(name)` lookup by exact name. `RemoteReply` gains
  `headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>` and `RemoteReply::new`; every
  struct literal in `app.rs` and `connection` now goes through `new`.
  `respond` writes the extra headers plus `Cache-Control: no-store` and
  `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on every JSON reply. `Limits.page`
  (120 a minute). In `connection`, an exact `GET` for a page path is
  answered there (`respond_page`: CSP, no-store, nosniff, no-referrer,
  `Connection: close`), followed by a TLS close_notify and the end of
  the connection, so the slot frees at once.
- **`src/adapters/web.rs`** (new): the `PAGES` table (path, type,
  `include_str!`), `CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY`, `PAGE_HEADERS`, `page()`;
  unit tests for the exact match, the page referencing only its own
  files or `data:`, no inline script/style/handler, no
  `innerHTML`/`eval`/`document.write` in the script, and a runner for
  `node --test web/app.test.js` that skips when node is absent (checked
  that it is not vacuous by breaking an assertion: the Rust test failed).
- **Host (`src/app.rs`).** `authenticate` takes the bearer, else the
  cookie `__Host-sb-<server_id>`; a cookie-only non-GET or upgrade needs
  `Origin == https://<Host>`, else 403 `origin` (refused unauthenticated,
  before `DeviceSeen`). `/pair` with `"transport": "cookie"` omits
  `token` from the body and sets
  `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`.
  `GET /api/v1/me` answers `{device_id, name, scope, server_id,
  server_name}`; not added to `capabilities`.
- **Core.** `core::remote::invite_url(identity, window, Option<IpAddr>,
  port)`: `https://<addr>:<port>/#code=…&key=…&id=…`, the loopback when
  `listen.lan` is off or there is no address, IPv6 bracketed. Core test.
- **Dialog (`src/ui/remote.rs`).** QR and "Copy invite" carry the URL;
  a Mac-only port shows "The port answers this Mac only; allow devices
  on the local network to pair a phone" in place of the address; the
  browser-trust sentence beside the redaction one. UI test rewritten.
- **Swift.** `PairingInvite.parse` accepts the URL (authority read as
  text so an IPv6 bracket survives) and still the JSON; a URL without
  `code`, `key` or `id` throws. Test added.
- **Page (`web/`).** `index.html`, `app.css`, `app.js`, `app.test.js` as
  the plan's UI section describes: fragment parse then `replaceState`,
  `/info` comparison, cookie pairing, `/me` on boot, the 401 inference
  from `/info`, list grouped and waiting first, last response for
  `kind: claude` else screen, reply box under `control` with no
  `prompt_refusal`, random-hex op kept across a retry, 3 s poll of
  `/waiting` (20 s while the socket is up), socket retry 5 s doubling to
  60 s, device name from the user agent. All routes in one `API` table
  of `'METHOD /path'` strings that `tests/remote.rs` reads.
- **Host tests (`tests/remote.rs`).** Page files and headers to an
  unpaired client, the JSON 404 for `/favicon.ico`, `POST /`, `/api`, a
  query not echoed; every route in the page's table answered with
  something other than `not_found`, and every `/api/v1/` in `app.js` in
  the table; cookie pairing end to end; two hosts' cookies kept apart and
  the bare `__Host-sb` refused; the `Origin` rule on send and on the
  upgrade (`subscribe_at` refactored over a new `subscribe_with` that
  takes headers); `/me` read → control → 401 after revoke with `/info`
  unchanged; rotation test now also checks `/info` gives the same id
  with another key; a page load freeing its slot; a page request failing
  at accept behind four stalled strangers; the 121st page request 429
  while `/info` and `/pair` are unaffected.
- **Spike `spikes/23-web-page/`** (README only) and its row in
  `spikes/README.md`.
- **Docs.** `docs/remote-client.md` §0 dated paragraph, §4.1 bound,
  §4.3 rows and the "anything else is `not_found`" sentence, the excerpt
  sentence at the old line 207 corrected, §5 (pre-pairing surface, QR as
  URL, token wording, a new "A browser" bullet with the cookie, `Origin`
  rule and the weaker trust, the spike-only line); `docs/design.md` dated
  bullet at the end of "Remote client" with its known gaps; `README.md`
  Layout rows and the dev-aid sentence; `client/README.md` invite
  wording; `CHANGELOG.md` Unreleased with the plan's line.

## Unresolved facts: built to the plan's fallback, not settled

- **Unresolved 1 (click-through for a SAN-less certificate).** Built
  the plan's default: certificate untouched, click-through is the trust
  step, said in the dialog without promising which browsers allow it.
  Note: facts.md's Settled "Certificate trust" says the plan "must build
  to" an IP SAN; the finalized plan explicitly chose not to (owner's
  choice) and I followed the plan.
- **Unresolved 2 (`wss://` on iOS).** Polling is the base; the socket
  only hastens it.
- **Unresolved 3 (cookie kept on a self-signed IP host).** Cookie
  transport built; the token-in-page fallback is not built (owner's
  call). Not tested in a browser.
- **Unresolved 4 (`replaceState` and history).** The page clears the
  fragment first thing; the code's single use is the rest.
- **Unresolved 6 (browser connection count).** Measured the host side
  only (below); the browser's own count is not measured.

## Spike

The browser questions (cookie storage and send, two ports' cookies, CSP
and `wss:`) were **not run**: no display session could be driven and the
repo forbids keystroke injection. The README gives the commands for the
owner. Five parallel connections against the test harness, five rounds,
were run with a temporary test (removed before the commit): every round
four got 200 and the fifth was reset at accept.

## What the plan got wrong or left out

- **Parallel requests from the page.** The plan's list step ("`/projects`,
  then `/projects/{id}/sessions` each") did not say sequentially, and
  the spike shows a fan-out would break: connections count as
  unauthenticated until their first authenticated reply, and a fifth at
  once is closed. `app.js` reads the sessions one project at a time on
  its kept connection; recorded in the spike and §4.1.
- **"About twenty literals".** There were 11 `RemoteReply` struct
  literals (10 in `app.rs`, 1 in `connection`), not about twenty.
- **`core::remote` was private.** `mod remote;` in `src/core/mod.rs` had
  to become `pub mod remote;` for the plan's `core::remote::invite_url`
  path.
- **`serve_remote` length.** Adding the `/me` arm took it to 101 lines,
  over pedantic `too_many_lines`; added a scoped
  `#[allow(clippy::too_many_lines)] // one arm per route`, the same
  pattern as `core/control.rs`.
- **`invite_url` signature.** The plan wrote `(identity, window,
  address, port)`; I made the address `Option<IpAddr>` and put the
  `listen.lan` choice inside it, so the UI holds no logic and the
  loopback case is testable in the core, as the plan's tests ask.
- **`subscribe_at` "takes extra headers".** Kept its signature and added
  `subscribe_with(port, headers, path) -> Result<Subscriber, String>`
  under it, so the refused upgrade can be asserted as an `Err`.
- **Node in this stage's shell.** `node --test` could not be run directly
  here (permission), but it runs through `cargo test`; verified that a
  failing JS assertion fails the Rust test.

I've built the plan as one commit on `stage/sb-230-implement-v5rev-opus-leanb`: `4b3a20c`, with the plan's commit message and its list of contract additions. It is not pushed and there's no pull request. `git status` is empty.

**Checks:** `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy` (pedantic, `-D warnings`) and `cargo test --locked --workspace` all pass, and the pre-commit hook passed too. On the Swift side I ran only `swift test --filter FixturesTests` (5 pass, including the new URL-parsing test), not the whole Swift suite. I skipped the Linux cross-check of `dispatch` because nothing platform-specific changed.

**What it does:**
- **The page:** the remote port now serves a small web page (`web/`: `index.html`, `app.css`, `app.js`) to anyone, with no build step and no dependencies.
- **The invite:** the pairing window's QR code and "Copy invite" now carry a URL, with the code, key and server id after the `#`, so the code never reaches a server. When the port answers only this Mac, the URL uses `127.0.0.1` and the dialog says so.
- **Pairing:** the page checks `/info` against the URL, then pairs and gets its token as a cookie its own script can't read. The cookie is named `__Host-sb-<server_id>` so two instances on one address don't overwrite each other.
- **Writes:** a request that carries only the cookie and changes something (or opens the events socket) must come from the page itself, or it gets a 403 `origin`.
- **New route:** `GET /api/v1/me` tells a device its own name and scope.
- **What the phone sees:** waiting sessions first, a session's last response or screen, and a reply box for devices allowed to send. It polls every 3 s, and the events socket only makes updates arrive sooner.
- **Swift client:** it parses the URL invite as well as the old JSON form.
- **Tests, docs and changelog:** the tests and docs the plan lists, plus the changelog line.

**Unresolved facts:** I built the plan's fallbacks and settled none of them:
- **Certificate:** unchanged, and clicking through the browser's warning is the trust step.
- **Cookies:** whether Safari and Chrome keep the cookie from this certificate on an IP address is untested. If they don't, keeping the token in the page instead is the owner's call, so I didn't build it.
- **Events socket on iPhone:** whether `wss://` connects there is untested. Polling covers it.

`facts.md` says the certificate must gain an IP subject alternative name, but the final plan deliberately leaves it alone, so I followed the plan.

**The spike** (`spikes/23-web-page/`): I couldn't run the browser questions, since there's no screen I can drive and the repo forbids keystroke injection. The README gives the owner the commands to run them by hand. I did measure five simultaneous connections against the test harness, with a temporary test I deleted before committing: every round, four were answered and the fifth was closed. The host only holds four connections that haven't authenticated yet.

**Where the plan was wrong or incomplete:**
- **Parallel requests:** fetching every project's sessions at once would hit that four-connection limit, so the page fetches them one at a time over its kept connection. The plan didn't say which.
- **Constructor sites:** there were 11 places building replies directly, not "about twenty".
- **Visibility:** `core::remote` was private, so I made it `pub mod` to give the plan's `core::remote::invite_url` path.
- **Function length:** adding the `/me` route took `serve_remote` one line over clippy's limit. I added a scoped allow, the same pattern used in `core/control.rs`.
- **`invite_url`:** it takes an optional address and decides the loopback case itself, so the dialog holds no logic and the core test can cover it.
- **Socket test helper:** I kept `subscribe_at` as it was and added `subscribe_with` (takes headers), so a refused upgrade can be checked as an error.
- **Node:** I couldn't run `node --test` directly in this shell, but `cargo test` runs it. I broke one assertion on purpose to confirm a JavaScript failure fails the Rust test.

All of this is also in the notes file at the path you gave.
